title: Faxian walks to India
hookLine: the monk Faxian set out on foot for India to find the rules of discipline (Legge, 1886)

cards: A monk in Chang'an has a problem with the rulebook. The monks' rules of discipline, the Vinaya, have reached China only in pieces. The books he can find are broken and incomplete, and he wants the whole rulebook.
He could wait for someone to bring the rest. Instead, he decides to go and get it himself, on foot, across a desert and over the mountains, all the way to India. And he writes it all down.

teach.b: First, the reason. Faxian's own record, which James Legge put into English, opens with it.

Living in Chang'an, he grieved that the books of discipline in China were broken and incomplete, so he and a few companions agreed to travel to India to seek the rules. Not treasure, not fame. The rulebook.
Second, the desert. His record describes a sea of sand with no birds overhead and no animals below, where you look all around and can't tell which way to go.
The only markers of the road, he writes, are the dry bones of travelers who died there. Third, the mountains.

Beyond the desert came high passes, snow in winter and summer, cliffs where the path was cut into the rock and the river ran far below. Along the way companions turned back, fell ill, or stayed behind in monasteries.
Fourth, India. He reached the places of the Buddha's life, the holy sites he had only read about, and settled down to study and copy texts of the discipline, so he could carry them home.
What makes his record matter is that it isn't a legend told by others. It's a traveler's own account, plain and specific, of what he saw: monasteries, customs, rulers, the state of the holy places.
Historians still read it for that reason. And at its center is one stubborn decision: he wanted the rules whole.

how: Buddhist monks and lay pilgrims still travel to the places of the Buddha's life in India and Nepal, and monastic communities study the Vinaya, the rules of discipline Faxian went to find.

practice: If you can, get up and walk to the far wall of the room or out the door, and then a few steps past where you'd usually stop; if you can't move right now, trace a route you know well in your mind and add one more street at the end.
Notice the moment you pass your usual turning point. Then rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Faxian. The Chinese monk who crossed desert and mountains on foot to find the complete rules of discipline, and wrote down what he saw.
